text_blocks.snippet: The First Continental Congress was a meeting of delegates from twelve of the thirteen American colonies (Georgia did not attend) in Philadelphia in 1774. It was convened in response to the Intolerable Acts, a series of punitive laws passed by the British Parliament after the Boston Tea Party. The Congress aimed to address colonial grievances and assert colonial rights, primarily through non-violent means like boycotts and petitions.
snippet_highlighted_words: a meeting of delegates from twelve of the thirteen American colonies (Georgia did not attend) in Philadelphia in 1774

list.title: Purpose:
list.snippet: The primary goal was to respond to the Intolerable Acts, which colonists saw as oppressive and a violation of their rights.

list.title: Key Actions:
list.snippet: The Congress adopted the Articles of Association, which called for a boycott of British goods starting December 1, 1774, unless the Intolerable Acts were repealed. They also drafted a Declaration and Resolves, outlining colonial rights and grievances and petitioning King George III.

list.title: Delegates:
list.snippet: Notable figures like George Washington, John Adams, Samuel Adams, and Patrick Henry were among the 56 delegates representing the colonies.

list.title: Significance:
list.snippet: The First Continental Congress marked a crucial step towards colonial unity and resistance against British rule. It demonstrated a willingness to act collectively to defend their rights and interests, laying the groundwork for future revolutionary action. While not calling for independence at this stage, the Congress set the stage for the Second Continental Congress, which would eventually declare independence.
